newsitem.title: IRAQ: U.N. food official sees imminent disaster in Iraq.
newsitem.headline: U.N. food official sees imminent disaster in Iraq.

text.p: Warning of an imminent food disaster for the poorest Iraqis, a U.N. official said on Sunday the condition of some children in hospitals in the sanctions-hit country was comparable to those he had seen in Somalia.
The U.N.'s World Food Programme (WFP) said its food supplies in Iraq had run out since October and that it had not received any confirmed pledges for new shipments.
Holdbrook Arthur, WFP's director in Iraq, said more than one million Iraqis were almost totally dependent on the U.N. food distribution system and he feared for their well-being.
"If we are not able to support this most vulnerable group...it would be a major disaster...It is pretty imminent," Arthur told Reuters.
"I have seen children in hospitals in Basra, Nassiriya and Amara (three southern Iraqi provinces) whose conditions are comparable to children I had seen...in Somalia," he said.

Before taking up his post in Iraq in August, Arthur was WFP's country director im Somalia, Rwanda, Burundi and Tanzania. Famine fuelled by war killed some 300,000 people in Somalia in the early 1990s before U.N.-sanctioned military intervention made an extensive international relief operation possible.
Iraq is under stringent U.N. trade sanctions imposed after its troops invaded Kuwait in 1990.
Humanitarian supplies are exempted from the sanctions, but the embargo on Iraq's oil exports means it has little cash to pay for them.

Arthur said the WFP launched an appeal on September 28 for about $19 million to help the most vulnerable Iraqis -- malnourished children under five, poor families, old women -- and orphanages and hospitals.
He said it had gathered $7.3 million for northern Iraq, but the food problem was the most acute in south-central Iraq, where only $500,000 had so far been donated -- by the Netherlands.
The food rationing system covers 1.4 million people in south-central Iraq and 600,000 in the north, Arthur said.
"The problem we are facing is that we are not getting support for the people located in south-central Iraq," he said.
Iraq and the United Nations signed a memorandum of understanding in May allowing Baghdad to sell $2 billion worth of oil in six months to raise money to buy food and medicine.
The pact was about to be implemented in September but was halted after Baghdad sent troops to northern Iraq to help one Kurdish faction fight a rival group.
"Even if we were to start the memorandum of understanding today...it would not cover the needs of these vulnerable people," Arthur said.
